idiom_name: hand-written tagged struct: enum tag plus union payload, built by ok()/err() helpers
implementation_notes: C has no sum type, so the classic structure is written by hand: a struct that keeps an enum tag next to a union of the two payloads (the tag is the only thing that makes reading the union defined), plus constructor helpers so that tag and payload can never drift apart, and a switch on the tag as the eliminator. The standard library's own precedent is a different shape - errno-style calls return a sentinel while the reason sits in a thread-local variable, and out-parameter APIs return a status code while writing the value through a pointer. Choose the tagged struct when the outcome must be stored, passed between layers or composed; keep the status-code plus out-parameter form when the caller only branches immediately.
pitfalls: Reading the union member that the tag does not name is type punning and undefined behaviour, and nothing checks the tag for you: build results only through the helpers and keep tag plus payload in one struct.

Returning the struct by value copies the payload - use an out-parameter plus a status enum for large values - and remember that errno is only valid immediately after a failing call, so save it before calling anything else.
C does not warn about an unhandled tag in a switch that omits a case unless you ask it to (-Wswitch-enum plus a default that aborts), so a newly added error can silently fall into the wrong branch.
